idiom_name: assertion functions (asserts x is T) plus validating accessors / parse-at-use
implementation_notes: TypeScript keeps the runtime check at the moment of use and adds a static half the dynamic languages lack: an assertion function (asserts x is Valid) or a type guard lets the check narrow the type, so everything after the gate is written against the validated shape, and a branded type stops a raw value from being substituted for a validated one. The accessor or Proxy form defers a single field's check to its read, while boundary parsing plus a use-named validation function is the better split for payloads whose expensive rules depend on the action. The classic validator-object tree is still justified when one rule set must serve many handlers, but for a single aggregate the assertion function plus the brand is the whole structure.
pitfalls: Assertion functions are unchecked against their body: a function declared asserts x is T that returns early will still narrow the type, so the implementation is the only source of truth and must be tested directly.
Validating getters fire on every read, including serialisation, logging and structuredClone, and a throwing accessor therefore breaks code paths that never intended to use the value.
Types vanish at runtime: a validated value passed into another module is only a cast if the brand is not enforced, so hand the branded type across boundaries instead of re-asserting it at each use.
